notes.b: The physical function meets the basic bodily needs of family members and protects those who cannot protect themselves.
points: The family provides food, warmth, shelter, clothing and rest for its members.
Procreation ensures the continuation of the population and gives children their first physical home.
The family protects dependants who are vulnerable, including young children, older people, the sick and people with disabilities.
Other social institutions supplement this function through local authority housing, GP and public health services, and school meals programmes.
The State supports the physical function through the medical card, housing supports, and home help services for older people.

notes.b: The economic function provides income and support for dependants, and links the family to the wider economy.
points: Adults earn income to support dependants, meaning children, and older children in full-time education.
Family members pay taxes and spend on goods and services, which supports the wider economy.
Historically, the farm or family business was a single economic unit in which every member worked.
Credit unions, banks and insurers supplement the family's financial management by offering savings, loans and cover against loss.
The Money Advice and Budgeting Service (MABS) helps families manage debt and plan their budgets.

The State supports this function through social welfare payments, including Child Benefit, the One-Parent Family Payment, the Working Family Payment (formerly Family Income Supplement), and carer's and disability allowances.

notes.b: The emotional function gives family members love, security and a sense of belonging.
points: A secure home gives children the emotional base from which they develop self-esteem.
Family members learn to express feelings and to form healthy relationships through daily interaction.
Parents act as role models and support each other, which helps children develop emotionally.
Counselling in schools, youth services and bereavement support supplement the family when it cannot meet emotional needs.
The State supports this function through parenting programmes and family support services run by community and voluntary groups.

notes.b: The educational function passes on skills, language and values, and prepares children for formal schooling.
points: The family is the primary educator, passing on beliefs, language, skills and customs through informal learning from birth.
Praise, encouragement and a stimulating home environment promote early intellectual development.
Parents support formal schooling through help with homework, reading together and educational outings.
Pre-school, primary and second-level schools, and third-level education, take over formal instruction as the child grows.
The State supports this function through the Early Childhood Care and Education (ECCE) scheme, free schooling, and special needs assistance in schools.

notes.b: The social function teaches children the norms, values and behaviour that allow them to live acceptably in society.
points: Through observation and imitation, children learn the norms, values and behaviour that society accepts.
Consistent discipline and fair boundaries help children develop self-control and respect for others.
Language, manners and social skills are learned at home before children enter school.
Schools reinforce socialisation through the hidden curriculum, and peer groups and youth organisations continue it.
When a family fails to socialise a child, the State can intervene, and the judicial system deals with individuals who do not conform.
Brainstorming: list each activity a family carries out in a week, then assign each one to a category.
Cooking a meal serves the physical function and also teaches table manners, which serves the social function.
Reading together serves the educational function and also the emotional function, by building closeness and confidence.
Paying bills and budgeting serve the economic function and teach children money management, which is part of the educational function.

keyTerms.definition: The family's role in meeting the basic bodily needs of its members and protecting dependants.
The family's role in providing income and financial support for its dependants.
The family's role in giving love, security and a sense of belonging.
The family's role in passing on skills, language, values and customs and preparing children for formal schooling.
The family's role in teaching children the norms and behaviour that allow them to live acceptably in society.
The lifelong process by which a person learns the norms, values and behaviour of their society.
A person who relies on another for financial support, such as a child or an older person who cannot work.
The unwritten lessons pupils learn at school, such as punctuality, respect for authority and how to behave with peers.
The biological production of children, which ensures the continuation of the population.
An accepted standard of behaviour within a society or group.
A State scheme providing a free pre-school year for children before they start primary school.

questions.prompt: Explain how the State assists the family with one of its functions.
questions.model: One function named, for example the economic function, and one or two State supports explained: Child Benefit as a regular payment that helps with the cost of raising children, and the Working Family Payment for low-paid working families. Any other accurate State support for the chosen function, such as ECCE for the educational function or parenting programmes for the emotional function, with an explanation of how it helps.

questions.prompt: Discuss the functions of the family in society, explaining how other social institutions supplement or take over each function.
questions.model: Physical: the family provides food, warmth, shelter and clothing and protects dependants; supplemented by housing, GP and public health services and school meals. Economic: the family provides income and support for dependants and pays taxes that support the economy; supplemented by social welfare payments and MABS. Emotional: the family gives love, security and self-esteem; supplemented by counselling services and parenting programmes. Educational: the family is the primary educator, passing on skills and customs and supporting homework; supplemented by pre-school, schools and the ECCE scheme. Social: the family teaches norms, values and discipline through observation and imitation; supplemented by schools through the hidden curriculum, peer groups and, where the family fails, the judicial system. Conclusion of the answer: the family remains the core institution for every function, with other institutions sharing or taking over the functions when families cannot meet them.
